title: A Recipe Sharing Feed
prompt: A recipe sharing app shows each user a home feed of recipes from the accounts they follow, newest first. Design the feed, using the full routine.
facts: About 20 million daily users, each opening the feed about 15 times a day; measured peak: 12,000 feed opens per second
About 2 million recipes are posted a day; measured peak: 200 posts per second. Accounts have 300 followers on average

Follower counts: 2,000 accounts have more than 100,000 followers, 300 of them more than 1,000,000, and the largest has 30 million. A user follows at most 2,000 accounts; at most 40 of them have more than 100,000 followers, and at most 10 more than 1,000,000
Fan-out workers add up to 300,000 feed entries per second in total, and at most 100,000 per second for one post
Feed cache nodes hold 64 GB each and answer about 100,000 lookups per second, each in about 2 ms; a post ID is 8 bytes. Fetching the content of 20 posts in one batch takes about 15 ms
Requirement: a new recipe appears in every follower's feed within 30 seconds of posting
Requirement: a feed page of 20 recipes loads within 150 ms, using at most 20 lookups in parallel, and the latest 500 recipes of the feed can be paged through
Requirement: the loss of any one cache node loses no feeds
scope: The home feed: posting, building and reading it
Ranking, comments and search are out of scope

requirements: States the 30-second freshness target, a page within 150 ms with at most 20 parallel lookups, paging through 500 recipes, and surviving one cache node
estimation: Push limit from freshness: 30 seconds × 100,000 per second = 3,000,000 followers; the 30-million account would take 300 seconds
Read limit: 20 lookups = 1 cached feed + at most 19 pulled accounts, so the threshold must leave each user at most 19 accounts above it: 100,000 allows up to 40, 1,000,000 at most 10
Write load below a 1,000,000 threshold: on average 200 posts per second × 300 followers = 60,000 per second at peak, under 300,000, with room for large posts

Cache: 500 IDs × 8 bytes = 4,000 bytes × 20 million users = 80 GB: at least 2 nodes, 4 with one replica each; reads 12,000 per second × up to 11 lookups ≈ 132,000 per second, about 66,000 per main node, under 100,000
design: API (post, getFeed with a cursor), data model (posts, the follow graph both ways, per-user feed of post IDs, recent post IDs per large account), a high-level design with a post service, fan-out queue and workers, feed cache, large-account cache and feed service, and a deep dive on the hybrid threshold and the read-time merge
data: A threshold from 1,000,000 to 3,000,000 followers, with both limits shown: at 100,000 a read could pull 40 accounts, and the facts bound the number only from 1,000,000 up
Merging by time with duplicates and unfollowed accounts dropped, and a cursor holding the oldest post ID shown
tradeoffs: Names failures with conditions, such as: fan-out workers fall behind and feeds get older while reads still work; a cache node fails and its replica takes over; an account near the threshold switching back and forth, prevented by a lower switch-back point; and a summary that checks each requirement

fullMarkDesigns: Design A, threshold 1,000,000. Requirements: every follower's feed has a new recipe within 30 seconds; a page of 20 within 150 ms with at most 20 parallel lookups; 500 recipes can be paged through; no feed lost with one cache node. Estimates: pushing works up to 30 × 100,000 = 3,000,000 followers; users follow at most 10 accounts above 1,000,000, so a read is at most 11 lookups; push load about 200 × 300 = 60,000 per second at peak, under 300,000; cache 500 × 8 bytes × 20 million = 80 GB, so 4 nodes with replicas, and about 12,000 × 11 = 132,000 lookups per second at most, about 66,000 per node even if only the 2 main nodes answer, under 100,000. API: post(content); getFeed(cursor) returns 20 recipes and the next cursor. Data: posts(id, author, created_at, content); follows indexed both ways; feed cache: latest 500 post IDs per user, split by user ID; large-account cache: latest 500 post IDs per account above 1,000,000. High-level: post service → posts store and fan-out queue → fan-out workers read followers and append the ID to each follower's feed, for authors at or below 1,000,000 followers; feed service → cached feed and each followed large account's list → merge → one batch fetch of content. Deep dive: an author with 1,000,000 followers is pushed in 10 seconds, well within 30; authors above it are pulled, so a read merges the cached feed with at most 10 lists, 11 lookups in parallel, about 2 ms, plus the 15 ms batch fetch, within 150 ms; the merge sorts by time, drops duplicate IDs and posts from unfollowed accounts, and returns a cursor with the oldest ID shown. An account switches to pull above 1,000,000 and back to push below 800,000. Failures: a backlog in the fan-out queue makes feeds older but reads keep working; an alert fires when the oldest queued post is 20 seconds old; a failed cache node's replica takes over. Summary: each requirement is met. Trade-off: 1,000,000 keeps reads small but pushes posts of accounts up to 1,000,000, which costs more writes than a lower threshold.

Design B, threshold 2,000,000. Requirements as in Design A. Estimates: pushing works up to 3,000,000 followers, so 2,000,000 meets the freshness target with each such post done in 20 seconds; users follow at most 10 accounts above 1,000,000, hence at most 10 above 2,000,000, so a read is at most 11 lookups; push load at peak about 60,000 per second plus a few large posts at 100,000 each, under 300,000; cache 80 GB on 4 nodes with replicas. API and data as in Design A, with the large-account cache holding accounts above 2,000,000. High-level: the same services, queue, workers and caches. Deep dive: authors up to 2,000,000 followers are pushed within 20 seconds; above it, followers pull, merging at most 10 lists with the cached feed, 11 parallel lookups plus the batch fetch, within 150 ms; the merge drops duplicates and unfollowed accounts and pages with a cursor. Switching: to pull above 2,000,000, back to push below 1,600,000. Failures: fan-out backlog, alerting when the oldest post has waited 20 seconds; cache replica takeover; an account crossing the threshold keeps its pushed posts, and the merge removes duplicates. Summary: each requirement is met. Trade-off: less room in the 30 seconds than Design A, so a backlog reaches the limit sooner, in exchange for fewer accounts to pull.

assumptions: Follower counts change slowly enough that the threshold check can use a count refreshed every few minutes
Follows are stored in a database indexed both ways
reference.design:
Requirements: a new recipe in every follower's feed within 30 seconds; a page of 20 within 150 ms with at most 20 parallel lookups; paging through the latest 500; no feed lost with one cache node.
Estimates: pushing one post at 100,000 per second meets 30 seconds only up to 3,000,000 followers; a read may pull at most 19 accounts, and users follow up to 40 accounts above 100,000 but at most 10 above 1,000,000; push load about 200 × 300 = 60,000 per second at peak, under 300,000; cache 500 × 8 bytes × 20 million = 80 GB, 4 nodes with replicas.
API: post(content); getFeed(cursor). Data: posts by ID; follows both ways; per-user feed of 500 post IDs in the cache; per large account, its latest 500 post IDs.
Design and deep dive: hybrid fan-out with a threshold of 1,000,000 followers (any value from 1,000,000 to 3,000,000 meets both limits; below 1,000,000 the facts give no bound on pulled accounts under 20): posts by smaller accounts are pushed through a queue and workers into followers' cached feeds within 10 seconds; posts by larger accounts are pulled at read time. A read merges one cached feed with at most 10 large accounts' lists, 11 parallel lookups and one batch fetch, about 17 ms; duplicates and unfollowed accounts are dropped; a cursor holds the oldest ID shown. Accounts switch to pull above the threshold and back to push only below 80% of it.
Failures: fan-out backlog makes feeds older but reads still work, with an alert at 20 seconds; a cache node's replica takes over; if both copies are lost, feeds are rebuilt by pulling. Summary: each requirement is met.
alternatives: Rejected: a threshold of 100,000, because a user may follow 40 accounts above it, needing 41 lookups, more than the 20 allowed
Rejected: pushing every post, because the 30-million account would take 300 seconds
Rejected: pulling every account, because a user may follow 2,000 accounts
